entries.title: The Best Digital Wall Calendar (2026): Skylight, Everblog, Apolosign
entries.summary: What originally looked like clutter turned out to be my new favorite gadget for organizing my family’s life.
entries.content:
I won’t lie to you: I hated the first digital wall calendar I tried.

I tested it last year and was left unimpressed. It was expensive and massive, and my calendar details were slow to appear (if they appeared at all). The device felt more like clutter than a useful addition to my home. So, I wrote off the idea of using a digital wall calendar, but to my surprise, they have only picked up in popularity and options since then. After trying a few new models myself this year, I can now see why.

These gadgets work by taking your online calendar—whether your Google Calendar, the calendar app on your iPhone, or your corporate Microsoft calendar account—and putting it on a digital screen that you can mount on the wall or prop up on a countertop or table. They’re often more than just calendars, also functioning as chore charts, meal planners, and sometimes even digital photo frames. I usually have smart displays all over my home, especially in my kitchen and living area, but for the past two weeks, I’ve replaced them all with digital wall calendars. And you know what? I don't miss talking to those annoying AI-powered assistants.

Instead, as someone who already lives and breathes by her Google Calendar, I love being able to see it on a large display in the middle of the kitchen, without needing my phone—especially when it’s on a digital wall device that immediately reflects my most up-to-date calendar. My husband and I have also been using the extra features more often, particularly to guide my 4-year-old through his evening bedtime routine with the help of his own companion device. Here's everything you need to know about the best digital wall calendars and whether they're right for you.

Updated August 2026: I've added the Skylight Buddy as a kid-friendly tool that includes some features of these digital calendar devices. I’ve also ensured accuracy and up-to-date information throughout.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

My Favorite Digital Calendars

What’s a Digital Wall Calendar?

You might have heard these gadgets called by various names. Maybe “digital wall calendar” or “smart calendar device.” Maybe you've just heard the name Skylight Calendar, which is a notably popular model right now. No matter what you call them, these devices all do the same thing: replace a paper calendar with a digitized one that connects to the calendar tools you're already using, like Google Calendar or Apple Calendar. The devices let you see your entire family’s schedule in one view, with the ability to update or add to it without needing a phone or a separate account. It also erases issues like unreadable handwriting and forgetting to write down an event you've already scheduled digitally, and its color-coding system makes it easy to see who's on the hook for which activities.

While these are often called wall calendars, you can usually choose to place them on a tabletop. I preferred the models that included a tabletop stand, but I was still able to prop up the ones that only came with wall-mounting hardware during my testing.

What Else Can a Digital Wall Calendar Do?

These devices aren't just calendars; they’re also designed for larger family management. You'll find features to help you plan meals, track to-do lists for multiple people, and earn rewards on a digital chore chart. The Skylight Calendar 2 is a favorite of mine because it includes a photo screensaver, but you'll need to be a Plus subscriber to get that and some of the other bonus features. Basically, you can use these calendars to manage your family's full schedule, chores, meals, and more in a single device.

Is a Digital Wall Calendar Worth It?

I didn't expect to feel this way, but having a physical version of my hyper-detailed Google Calendar in the center of my home has been a delight. My husband and I both check our calendar at a glance while we're chatting in the kitchen, and at the start of the week, we'll camp out in front of it for a few minutes to plan the week's dinners and grocery needs. My top pick, Skylight Calendar 2, actually prompts us to add items to our grocery list based on what meals we picked (if it's a stored recipe, that is).

My husband and I have found it so useful in part because we're both good about adding events to our individual calendars, so now this device can reflect that work. It lets us skip pulling out our phones when discussing plans for the next day or the upcoming weekend.

The Best Digital Calendars

Skylight's calendar is the most popular for a reason. The brand is known for its digital photo frames, and now you can use the same Skylight app to operate any of its three digital calendars: The older 10-inch Calendar ($170), the newer Calendar 2 ($320), and the Calendar Max ($630). The main difference between these is size, but Calendar 2 is the newest model, with improved performance and interchangeable Snap Frames ($30 to $50) you can purchase to change the device's look.

What makes Skylight great is its software. It's easy to use, and it quickly imported my Google Calendar and the wide variety of calendars shared to it, so I could immediately add all of my family's schedules to the device. The left-side menu bar shows all the pages you can toggle between. Calendar, Lists, Tasks, Rewards, Meals, and Recipes are the main areas you'll use; you can also access the Photos, Sleep, and Settings pages from the same menu.

The app and device interface are clean and intuitive compared with other models, many of which feel like Android tablets with a fancy calendar mode added. I was able to easily assign calendars I created on the device to family members. For example, I assigned my husband's calendar to him without needing him to log in or import it, and I could have assigned any calendar I created to my son as well. I also liked that shared events only appear once on the Skylight, but with both of our designated colors added to show the event in question applied to both of us.

Lists and Tasks sound similar, but Tasks are meant to function as a chore chart, connecting back to the Rewards page to build habits and earn the reward you set after hitting a certain goal. The main audience for this is children who are old enough to check the calendar. Lists are for things like your groceries. If you add recipes to the Recipe tab and then add those to your meal plan for that week, Skylight will offer to put the corresponding ingredients on your shopping list.

The downside of Skylight is the paywall. To access some of the best features—meal planning, rewards, photo screensaver, and the in-app AI assistant tool Sidekick—you'll need to be a Plus subscriber for either $79 a year or $8 a month. Having this device double as a digital photo frame makes it worth the cost to me. I love getting to have my two favorite things nearby: photos of my family and instant access to our shared calendars.

The Everblog HomeCal has an operating system that feels pleasantly similar to the Skylight. It has a bit of an Android undertone to it, but it doesn't feel like a giant tablet as much as the Apolosign or Cozyla calendars (both below). Setup was pretty seamless, but there was a delay for the device to update with my calendar invites. It would also take a while for the Everblog to reflect changes I made to my Google Calendar on another device. While it worked well for the most part during testing, I occasionally noticed events missing from my Everblog. It also turned each calendar email account I connected to the device into a separate profile, which was annoying. I could toggle off the extra emails when I was on pages outside of the calendar, though, so I didn't have three profiles for myself on my Chores page, for example.

The menu on the left-hand side is very similar to Skylight's, with options like Calendar, Chores, and Meal Plan. There isn't a recipe section, which I miss, but there is a Fridge section, which lets you track the groceries you already have. Part of why this exists is because Everblog also has a smaller, battery-powered version of this calendar that's designed to attach to your fridge, aptly named the FridgeCal ($249). Still, I prefer the Recipe tab on the Skylight. The Everblog also has a Chores tab, but no additional tab for tracking regular chores or other to-dos separately.

There's a free photo option, but the uploader tool in the app only lets you add one photo at a time. Painful, but I'm sure many would feel it's worth the free price tag. To use the feature, you'll need to go into the settings on the physical device to turn on photo slideshow as your screensaver. The Everblog defaults to pinging loudly at the start of any calendar event, which you can only change on the device, not in the app.

There's a button on the bottom right-hand corner of the screen that will take you to a homepage with an overview of the calendar and chores, and access to other applications like Spotify and Netflix, if you set up your accounts on this device for streaming content. It comes enabled for wall mounting, but you can purchase the Calendar Stand ($39) if you want to situate it on a tabletop, and there's a wooden frame ($99) you can buy to snap on to give it a nicer look.

Apolosign's digital calendar has three sizes: 15.7, 21.5, and 27 inches. It runs Google's Android OS, so it operates very similarly to an Android tablet and to Google's Pixel Tablet, if you've used either as a smart display, as I have. The Apolosign has two modes: Calendar and Android. Calendar mode worked similarly to Skylight. I seamlessly connected it to my Google Calendar, imported over most of my various shared calendars, and color-coded them.

The Calendar mode has a left-side menu bar (you'll have to tap to make it appear), with sections for Home, Calendar, Routines, To-Dos, Rewards, and Meals. The Home page has a two-column design, showing you the calendar on one side and your Routines and To-Dos on the other. You can then tap into any of these sections or check off items directly from the Home page. Apolosign also has baked-in notifications that chime to remind you about calendar events and to-dos, plus phone notifications to let you know how many items are on your calendar that day.

WIRED Reviewer Kat Merck also tested Apolosign, but used Android mode instead of Calendar mode. Android mode allows you to customize widgets and layout, so she opted for a monthly view. This mode also lets you use photos from Google Photos as a background and screensaver. She says it's nice to be able to customize the layout in this mode, but it struggles to sync with other programs, including Apolosign's own app.

I don't like the Apolosign experience quite as much as the Skylight or Everblog, and Kat agreed that this device is not very intuitive and takes a lot of patience to set up. But having no paywall is a huge plus, and many people will feel it's worth getting used to the more Android-style experience to not pay a monthly or yearly fee. But since it's essentially a large Android tablet, iPhone users have flagged on Reddit that they can't two-way sync between it and their iPhone devices. The Apolosign is often on sale for the same price, if not cheaper, than the Skylight.

If you want a version made for kids, Skylight has something along those lines called the Skylight Buddy (8/10, WIRED Recommends). It's not a digital calendar but rather a chore-and-routine display that helps kids visualize and check off their daily to-dos without needing to navigate an entire family calendar.

My 4-year-old loves his 7-inch Buddy, and it really does help get him to brush his teeth and put on his PJs in a timely (well, more timely) fashion now that it's in his room. It also has a night-light and sound machine, but the sounds are limited, and the night-light is pretty dim. So for those capabilities, I'm sticking to the Hatch Baby my son is used to and loves.

Ultimately, this is most useful if you already have and use a Skylight Calendar. That’s because the Buddy can sync to and show designated tasks already on the Skylight Calendar. But even if you don't have the Calendar and just want more of a routine tool or chore-tracker for your child, this is a really good option. There are subscription options to get more features—Buddy Plus is $39 a year, and Skylight Plus is $79 a year. Skylight Plus is what you should get if you have the Calendar, as it unlocks paywalled features for both devices. But I haven't needed any subscription-only capabilities to keep my son excited about and engaged in his bedtime routine.

Others I’ve Tested

Cozyla Calendar Plus 2 (15.6 Inches) for $350: This calendar is similar to Apolosign with an Android-based operating system, but it didn't import my shared calendars, meaning it took more work to set up. It was overall frustrating to navigate and didn't guide me through its tools as effectively as Skylight or Apolosign. While Cozyla doesn't have any subscription fees, its 15.6-inch size is more expensive than both Skylight's and Apolosign's.

Hearth Display for $699: This is another digital calendar and family tool that has a paywall with an affordable Family Membership ($6 a month) but a much higher initial price point. It's only available in a large, 27-inch size, and I found it was slow to load my calendar and also bulky compared to more affordable options.

FAQs

How Do Digital Wall Calendars Work?

Digital wall calendars sync with your existing digital calendar app of choice, like Google Calendar, and display it on the physical screen. There are usually additional tools for recipes, to-do lists, and chores, but each digital wall calendar varies in how you import the information. You may have to manually import it or type the details into the device, but once you get used to the process, the function can be helpful for the whole family.

Will Changes to My Calendar Appear Instantly?

Changes you make on your native calendar app, like Google Calendar and Apple's Calendar, should reflect quickly onto the digital wall calendar device. But changes you make on the device aren't always backward compatible with the native calendar. It depends on the calendar's settings and how the information was shared; I can edit my primary personal calendar on the Skylight Calendar 2, for example, but I can’t edit my work calendar that I shared to the Skylight through my personal. There are also some syncing issues you may run into with the Apolosign, which doesn't two-way sync with an iPhone since the digital calendar runs on an Android operating system.

How Is a Digital Calendar Different From a Smart Display?

Many smart displays look similar to these devices but have an entirely different operating system. Sure, the Google Pixel Tablet has some overlap with the Apolosign and Cozyla, since they all run an Android operating system. But unlike smart displays, digital calendar devices are designed with specific tools to run your family and none of the clutter. You'll lose out on smart-home support, though Apolosign claims you can use Google Assistant on it (that hasn't worked for me so far). On most devices, you'll also compromise on extras like video streaming (you can, however, stream on Everblog). But as someone who uses a smart display regularly, I really didn’t miss it once I switched over to the digital calendar device. I do wish there were a weather-report page, as most digital wall calendars just show the current weather.

Does It Have to Go on the Wall?

No—in fact, most of these devices come with a table-stand option. I only tested in table-stand mode since I had multiple of these devices in my house at one time, but the wall-mounting option is nice, allowing you to keep your tabletops clear. The 15-inch models are great for tabletops, and you may want to consider larger sizes for the wall-mounting route.

entries.title: I Tried a Window-Cleaning Robot: Do Not Recommend
entries.summary: I tested the top-of-the-line Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni window-cleaning robot on my Victorian home, and it was an unmitigated disaster.
entries.content:
I love the idea of robots taking over menial tasks, so I was excited to try the Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni. This premium window-cleaning robot is highly rated online. I have a robot vacuum and a robot mower, and I would never go back to doing these chores myself. Sadly, I had such a traumatically awful experience with the Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni that I’m left wondering why anyone would want a window-cleaning robot at all.

Before I embark on this tale of woe, I should point out that most of my issues are with the whole category, not the Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni specifically. There are circumstances where I can imagine it working well. I briefly tested another window-cleaning robot, the much cheaper Mova N1 ($199), for comparison, and can attest that the Ecovacs has a much smarter design and cleans more efficiently. It might even be the best window-cleaning robot you can get; I just don’t think a robot for cleaning windows is worthwhile for most homes.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

The Good

The Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni has a smart design and comes in a charging case that includes its own battery. The case has slots and compartments for cables, spare pads, cleaning solution, and the bot itself, attached with a retractable, braided, 18-foot cable. It looks like a little cooler with a folding handle and weighs around 15 pounds. A full charge gives you 110 minutes of cleaning.

The Winbot is 10 by 10 by 2.5 inches and weighs around 4 pounds. You attach a cleaning pad to the Velcro sections and fill it with the cleaning solution. It has a leatherlike strap for picking it out of the case and sticking it to the window. Press the button on the front to start it up. It takes a few seconds to ramp up the suction, then tells you when it’s firmly in place, so you can let go. This is a nerve-racking moment the first few times, but the suction is plenty powerful.

You can press a button on the case to cycle through the four modes. There are Deep and Thorough modes, recommended for exterior windows, Fast mode for interior windows, and an Edge Cleaning mode. I was surprised by how quick and easy it was to set up, and I started with the biggest window in our house, a recently installed, ground-level, modern window at the back, roughly 7 by 10 feet.

The Winbot navigated to the top using its tank-style tracks and then cleaned in horizontal lines. It has wee bumpers that detect the edges, and it deploys an occasional spurt of cleaning fluid onto the glass ahead of it. The cleaning pads are microfiber pads. The Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni did a decent job on this first window. If you have a lot of large windows like this, it might be worth looking at. My only complaints were that it left a dirty residue in the corners and smearing in places.

I had it clean my back door next, which is a large pane of glass, but it struggled with the handle. I was surprised to find that, after cleaning the inside and outside of the first window and door, it asked me to change the pad and refill the cleaning solution. It comes with one spare pad, and you can flip them over, though you will quickly end up with muck in the Velcro if you do.

My Victorian house has tall bay windows, and I was excited to try the Winbot there next. I struggle to reach the top of these windows. I have tried a ladder and an extending cleaning pole, but neither is ideal. I figured the Winbot might just be the solution. I was wrong.

The Bad

I have a traditional sash-and-case bay window, recently replaced at great expense. I tried the Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni on the largest, top-central pane first. It mostly cleaned the inside but got stuck on the metal loop fittings for opening the window and had to give up. I tried it on the outside. It was slow, but it eventually cleaned most of the window, except for a clag of muck in the corners and dirty stripes down the edges. Unfortunately, when it got to the bottom, it did a weird stuttering maneuver, managing to damage the astragal by ripping off paintwork.

OK, so window-cleaning robots cannot deal with traditional windows. I know textured glass interferes with the suction and, predictably, handles and fixtures interfere with the movement, but it also struggles with astragals that aren’t thick or solid enough. I wouldn’t risk using it with any that aren’t finished in hard plastic or something else durable.

I figured I’d give it one last chance on the upstairs bay window, as it’s a PVC replacement that was put in before we moved in, so it has thicker astragals finished in hard plastic. Using it one story up gave me serious anxiety. After an alarming five minutes or so of watching it loudly and squeakily navigate the window, it began to sound an alarm and flash a red light, with a stern voice informing me it was stuck and I should check the app for solutions. Where was it stuck? You guessed it, right at the top of the window where I had no hope of reaching it.

I’m not ashamed to say I panicked. I worried that if it suddenly fell, it would potentially smash into the window downstairs. The charging case does act as a counterweight; other window-cleaning bots have tethers to attach to furniture. There’s also a button to retract the cord and cut the slack, but there’s still potential for damage if it falls. I tried to lean out of my window, while it loudly alerted, to see if I could reach the release button. No joy.

By this time, a couple of passersby had stopped to watch. I tried to pull it in using the cable, but it wouldn't budge. Eventually, I figured out I could lower the top pane just enough to reach it. But pressing and holding the button to power down the suction, while hanging out my window and holding the strap, felt downright dangerous. My heart was pounding in my ears by the time it finally released. I got it inside and back into its case, where it will remain until I return it.

The Ugly

Reflecting on this sorry saga, I can't help feeling, even without my mishaps, which may be partly down to user stupidity and bad luck, that window-cleaning robots are just a massive waste of time.

They're way too much work to use. Time-wise, I could clean the windows far faster and do a better job with less stress. By the time you’ve set up a window-cleaning robot and stuck it on the window, you could have cleaned it yourself. You have to babysit the damn thing and then detach it and move it to the next window. Even if you get to a point of trusting it, you’ll have to return every five to 10 minutes. It can’t deal with window handles, fittings, or certain astragals, and windows must be at least 12 by 16 inches, but realistically larger, for it to be worth using. It always leaves dirt in the corners and cannot remove stubborn stains like bird droppings.

Using it on upstairs windows is harrowing. Leaning outside to retrieve it feels dangerous. It also goes through cleaning solution and dirties up the pads very quickly. I’d probably need eight pads if I wanted to clean all my windows in one go, and the 230-milliliter bottle of solution provided would maybe last me three full washes. Of course, both the extra pads and the solution are overpriced ($30 for 1 liter of cleaner and $20 for two pads), and the manual warns you not to use anything else.

It’s also loud. I measured 68 decibels when cleaning. When I used it on my front windows, several people heard it and stopped to stare. The universal reaction from family, friends, and strangers was bemusement. No one seemed to think a window-washing robot was a good idea.

Now, if you live high up in an apartment with large, modern windows and there’s no window-cleaning service, it could be great, though attaching and detaching it will be scary. I also wondered if it might be handy for folks with mobility issues, but it’s actually quite a lot of work to use. There are scenarios where I can see potential value, but for the average home, I don’t think it’s worth it. As for me, I’m done with window-cleaning robots forever.

entries.title: ‘Your Excel Skills Suck’: The Power Users Turning Spreadsheets Into a Spectator Sport
entries.summary: Data and finance professionals are competing in Excel obstacle courses—amassing huge followings and keeping the Microsoft program relevant.
entries.content:
For many people, Microsoft Excel is to be avoided at all costs.

Maybe you lied about being “proficient” with the spreadsheet program to pad out your résumé and have lived in fear of being found out ever since. Or it could be that you do have a grasp on a few basic formulas but find the interface too labyrinthine to truly master.

Still, like it or not, Excel remains an integral part of businesses, with Microsoft claiming “hundreds of millions” of users worldwide. But for a thriving community of content creators, Excel’s uses go far beyond practicality. They live for the thrills of ninja-like Excel efficiency, and they’re happy to impart their esoteric knowledge to those brave enough to seek it out. They amass huge fandoms by demonstrating their flair for unexpected productivity hacks and posting record times on “obstacle runs,” with some even competing in official Excel championships for prize money (and bragging rights).

Vying for spreadsheet glory is just part of the fun, however. At the end of the day, everyone really wants to help each other get better.

Dan Kidney, 32, in London, tells WIRED he “accidentally” leveled up his Excel skills while working as an insurance data analyst and building his own ecommerce company from scratch, though he never expected to teach others the tricks he’d picked up in that time.

“I decided to start using my spare time to post on TikTok as an experiment during a planned employment break,” he explains, first sharing videos covering the Excel functions a beginner should know. A few weeks in, Kidney posted footage of himself racing through the varied challenges of an Excel obstacle course he’d designed himself—and engagement suddenly exploded, pushing the clip to 1 million views within days. Commenters replied that he had completed each page before they’d even had time to read the instructions on it.

Today, Kidney has a combined 300,000 followers on Instagram and TikTok accounts, both called “Functional Excel,” and his speedruns have had a surprising impact beyond his own office. He says a schoolteacher in rural Germany saw his videos and assigned his students to practice Excel on his templates, leading to a class competition.

“Your Excel skills suck,” says Jonathan Tristan, a 29-year-old content creator known as “Your Finance Brother,” in a video recently posted to his TikTok and Instagram pages. Like other influencers in the space, Tristan, who is based in Los Angeles and was previously an investment banker, advocates for dispensing entirely with the mouse and relying only on a flurry of keyboard combination moves to navigate Excel. And he goes one step further: “Pop the F1 key off your keyboard,” he instructs his viewers.

Excel’s power users end up with “stylistic preferences,” Tristan says, and ditching the F1 key is an example of a choice that is both practical and something of a flex. “A really common shortcut you'll use is that you'll basically toggle between the Escape and the F2 key to see what your formula is doing in Excel,” he explains. The problem is that if you accidentally hit F1, which sits between those keys, it brings up a help menu, slowing down your work. (Plus, would a genuine operator ever need help?)

Tristan, who has shared his own impressive Excel speedruns, says he imparts this kind of wisdom to his approximately 700,000 followers because every minute counts when you’re working around the clock on Wall Street—going 10 percent faster if you spend 10 hours a day in Excel, he says, is the difference between “getting five hours of sleep versus six hours of sleep.”

Of course, apart from wanting to clock out earlier, Excelheads are increasingly motivated by a sense of friendly rivalry and the prestige that comes with flawless control over their screens.

“The obstacle courses and speedruns have added another layer to that since you can directly compare times, find better ways to accomplish the same task, and directly compete against each other,” says Drew Koontz, 29, the data analyst behind the tutorial website Encyclopedia Excel. He points out that Excel has become an unlikely esport: Last December in Las Vegas, Diarmuid Early of Ireland—described by some as the “LeBron James of spreadsheets”—won the 2025 Microsoft Excel World Championships, fending off Andrew Ngai of Australia, who won the tournament three times in a row from 2021 to 2023.

According to Koontz, speed is far from the only way to distinguish oneself in the Excel community. He shouts out engineer George Lungu, the administrator of the web page Excel Unusual, where he demonstrates how the program can be leveraged to create sophisticated animations and more. It’s “probably the most impressive collection of Excel works on the internet,” Koontz says. “He’s built fully working flight simulators, physics engines, roller coasters, planet simulations—it’s crazy.”

Ask an Excel influencer to name someone they credit with expanding the scene, and they’re more than likely to mention Ryan Park. Through his Excel Obstacle Course tutorials and videos, the Cincinnati-based father and data scientist, 49, estimates that he has helped “tens of thousands” of people improve their Excel productivity by gamifying the program.

Park’s Excel expertise came from years of correcting 401(k) data for a company whose clients all had their own methods of arranging spreadsheets. “The processors had to get good at cleaning and reorganizing data with 100 percent accuracy and as fast as possible,” he says. “I loved playing video games like Street Fighter II as a teenager, because learning the ‘special moves’ was so satisfying. That’s how I view the shortcuts I teach—they are the ‘special moves’ of Excel.”

It wasn’t until his coworkers began to comment on his speed that Park realized he was a bit of a savant. “I think there’s something hypnotic about watching someone use Excel without the mouse,” he says. “The clicks and cells flying around have this weird universal appeal.” As he researched Excel content on social media, he found it mostly “boring” and decided to start selling an obstacle course he’d designed for himself and his friends.

Now Park has around 300,000 followers; he’s amused that this audience is a mix of “students” and straight-up fans. “I get comments that say it was soothing to watch or that it gives them ‘tingles,’” he says of the latter group. In an era when tedious labor is commonly delegated to artificial intelligence systems, perhaps there is a heightened pleasure in seeing a real human being match the precision of a machine. Park, for one, brushes off replies about Excel being “so 20 years ago” or claiming that AI could finish a given task in mere seconds. “My response is that I’d be done before they can even explain the desired outcome to an AI tool,” he says.

As for Excel itself, Park doesn’t believe it’s going anywhere: “It’s like saying that pen and paper will be obsolete,” he says. “No way.”

entries.title: We Bought a $500 Counterfeit Rolex So Good, Even Rolex Didn’t Spot It
entries.summary: The replica watch industry is in its “super clone” era. Following tips from murky internet forums, we bought three budget fakes that were good enough to pass as real—but ultimately disposable.
entries.content:
“Would you like a glass of champagne?” Even though I'm painfully thirsty and nervous beyond belief, I decline the salesperson's offer.

I’m sitting upstairs in Rolex’s flagship London store on Old Bond Street. I’ve just handed over a fake Rolex to the staff and requested that its bracelet be adjusted, a simple bit of maintenance that requires removing a few links. I haven’t volunteered that the watch is a phony, but I haven’t said it’s legit, either.

My imposter Oyster Perpetual is now on a workbench in the glass-fronted servicing room on the second floor. I can see staff in white lab coats working diligently as a salesperson joins them to carefully examine the timepiece before downsizing the metal bracelet.

This replica is one of a few WIRED has purchased on the internet. So far, nobody in the store has spotted that the watch is a fake. Surely the game's about to be up? Maybe there’s just time to slip away before the police are called.

After what feels like far too long, the salesperson returns. He, like his colleagues downstairs did when I arrived, congratulates me on a beautiful watch and hands me back the counterfeit timepiece, now perfectly sized. The removed links have been placed reverently in a delicate, tiny paper bag, marked with the Rolex logo in cadmium green. Heart still pounding, I walk out.

Purchasing a counterfeit Swiss watch used to mean haggling at a Canal Street market stall or ducking into a Hong Kong back alley, where an approximation of a Rolex, Patek Philippe, or Audemars Piguet could be picked up for $50. If it survived beyond the flight home, that felt like a bonus. Now, though, the era of the “super clone” has arrived.

Mass-produced in huge quantities by Chinese factories, these watches are sold through dealers who advertise on TikTok and Instagram, broker through WhatsApp, and arrange discreet delivery to your door. Since reputation by word-of-mouth is paramount (these businesses can’t exactly show their wares in a digital shop window), they even claim to offer customer service channels, warranties, repair centers, and guarantees to send a replacement if your purchase is seized by customs.

In dedicated forums on Reddit and other websites, strictly moderated communities spread gossip about factories being raided by authorities, offer sketchy legal advice, upvote buyers’ photos of fake Rolexes worn behind the wheels of Lamborghinis, and even offer quality control services.

Quality control, or QC, is at the heart of this community. The subreddit r/RepTime has 269,000 weekly visitors and over 18,000 weekly contributions, according to Reddit’s own statistics. Posts about new counterfeit watch purchases pile up by the hour, both in r/RepTime and r/RepTimeQC, the offshoot subreddit focused on quality control. The posts contain photographs sent from the dealer to the customer, who then seeks advice from the RepTime community on whether they should “GL” (green-light) or “RL” (red-light) their purchase.

Every post must follow a strict format, demonstrating that the buyer has put effort into understanding the QC process and assessing their own watch before seeking the approval of the community and its moderators. As with other high-traffic subreddits, new accounts cannot post right away and instead must earn comment karma by communicating in other, more open subreddits first. Without that, posts are automatically intercepted and deleted before they appear in public and pollute the feed.

The posts are stuffed with coded language. Beyond the usual watch-world reference numbers and model nicknames (like a 124060 Sub, or a “Hulk” and “Pepsi”), there are factory names, often abbreviated to two or three letters, and aliases of every TD, or “trusted dealer.”

There’s earnest talk of gaps around the SELs (solid end links of a bracelet), the shortening of “genuine” and “replica” to “Gen” and “Rep,” and an aesthetic grading system for the cloned watches going from “1:1,” “Super Rep,” and the best of the best, “NWBIG,” which stands for “Not Worth Buying in Gen”—replicas considered so accurate that buying the genuine article is deemed entirely unnecessary.

The insidery shop talk might appeal to the devotees, but it doesn't exactly disguise what's going on—not that some community members seem to care about the potential illegality of replica timepieces. Numerous claims of shipments being intercepted and seized are batted away with advice to ignore letters received from customs.

Despite hundreds of quality-control requests landing in the subreddit every month, one source tells us that 98 percent of them are picked up by just three moderators. “Helping people with our comments is what we truly enjoy, and it’s the reason we spend so much time on the sub,” says one moderator, who asked to remain anonymous due to their fear of legal repercussions. They add that one of the group’s moderators “is a professional watchmaker,” but that others are amateurs in the field.

Are they concerned about the ethical implications of what they are doing? “I’m in the USA, and it is not illegal to buy or own replica watches,” the moderator says. “It is illegal to sell a replica and claim it is genuine. I am very strongly opposed to that. In fact, on the rare occasion that someone mentions more than a passing interest in a replica watch I am wearing, I volunteer that the watch is a replica.”

Even a Reddit community with more than a quarter of a million weekly visitors represents a mere fraction of the global fake-watch industry. The Federation of the Swiss Watch Agency has estimated that tens of millions of fake watches are produced every year, dwarfing the number legitimately manufactured by Swiss brands. And, while many super clones sell for between $500 and $700, there are cases of ultra counterfeits posing as watches worth millions.

“There’s a very well-known Patek,” says counterfeit watch expert Adrian Hailwood, referring to an automatic model with the reference number 3448. It was the first serially produced automatic perpetual calendar wristwatch, and there have long been rumors that two examples were made in rose gold for a South American retailer. Only one is publicly known, a 1968 example first sold in Uruguay. In 2011 it was sold at auction by Christie’s for CHF 2,099,000 (about $2.3 million at the time), then sold again in 2025 for CHF 2.7 million (about $3.3 million).

“Allegedly there’s another one,” Hailwood says. “But I’ve seen three—all pretending to be that one, and all of them with faults. So somebody is churning out rose gold 3448s. And if it’s potentially got a list price of a million pounds, there’s a lot of incentive to put them together.”

Hailwood says that because such a piece would have real Patek innards and a totally fake outside, requiring a lot of work and resources and access to parts, each would cost between £20,000 to £30,000 to create. “You can imagine someone going, ‘Look, we can’t put this through public auction, it would be a million pounds. But, say, £400,000 and ask me no more questions.’ People with more money than sense would potentially go for that,” he says.

Million-dollar Pateks tend not to crop up on r/RepTime. Instead, the vast majority of watches subjected to quality control checks are replica Rolexes. Posts scrutinizing the fine details of Submariners, Datejusts, and Daytonas are especially frequent, along with a smattering of Tudor, Omega, IWC, and Cartier replicas. Most tend to be stainless steel, since their low manufacturing cost means these clone watches cannot be made from real precious metal.

QC photos are taken after a watch has been produced and paid for, usually with cryptocurrency sent from buyer to dealer. The aim of the QC photo is to show the dial from dead center, which helps the customer check for common faults such as misaligned hour markers. This is done by drawing lines on the images between markers to check that they are level, or by using an online tool that has premade ruler templates for the most popular Rolexes.

Helpfully, QC posts include the names of the dealer and factory, the model of watch, and a set of checks for index alignment, dial printing, date wheel alignment if applicable, hand alignment, and bezel. They often include data on the watch’s movement, shown in a dealer-produced video of the piece being tested on a timing device known as a timegrapher. Dealer contact details and links to websites advertising counterfeit products are not shared—and Reddit has removed some content for violating its trademark policy—but it only takes a couple of clicks to find exhaustive purchasing guides elsewhere.

As long as the poster has done their homework and provided a thorough assessment of the watch, a moderator will respond with feedback like: “You did a pretty good job with the QC tool. Index aligns superbly and the bars are straight. Bezel engraving is solid and dial printing strong. Bezel pip looks centered and SELs are good with maybe the bottom right one showing its pin in one pic … [timegrapher] numbers are within range. If you’re ready to GL, GL and wait for the magic box to arrive. Enjoy.” Some responses are more blunt: “All good, but you knew that. GL.”

Amazingly, the aesthetic standard of these super clone replicas is so high that almost every QC’d watch gets a green light. In the rare event of a red light—one mod estimates that RLs are recommended only 5 percent of the time—the buyer asks the seller for another replica, which is often offered up without much protest.

Buying Time

To test for ourselves just how easy buying super clones actually is, WIRED followed the online advice of the Reddit communities to buy three different clone Rolexes of our own from a dealer called “JTime.”

We chose two classics, a replica Submariner for $438 and a Daytona at $768—plus, in an attempt to throw a wrench in the gears, one potentially harder to duplicate accurately, an Oyster Perpetual “Celebration” with its intricate multicolored bubble dial for $498.

The Sub and Daytona were classified on the community’s master spreadsheet as being NWBIG. The Celebration was listed a step below at “VG,” or very good. We had to contact JTime through WhatsApp and pay using the stablecoin USDT (though some dealers, including ours, take credit card payments if you’re feeling particularly foolish). Two of our watches would be ordered from one factory called Clean, with the Celebration model from another called VSF. Both are in China.

A few days after sending JTime a screenshot of the successful crypto transfer, email photos came through showing our watches. All three looked immaculate, even the Celebration model. After earning enough Reddit karma to post (which took some time, meaning we had to stall our dealer), we dropped the dealer images on RepTime’s QC channel for evaluation, hoping to get a thumbs-up from the apparent king of quality assessors, “WatchYoda,” whose opinion seems to carry considerably more weight than any other.

Sadly, perhaps feeling a disturbance in the force, WatchYoda didn't engage on our posts, but other assessors gave our pieces the GL.

Within weeks, cardboard boxes arrived with shipping labels claiming the contents to be men’s polyester pants worth $15. All three watches were protected by plastic wrapping and rubber bezel guards bearing the factory name. The Celebration even came with an obviously fake Rolex warranty card.

All three arrived as aesthetically described by JTime, looking remarkably genuine, even down to micro-adjustment mechanisms in their bracelets, and all kept accurate time.

However, one vital detail slipped through the super-clone QC process unchecked: We ordered a 36-mm Oyster Perpetual Celebration, but what arrived was a 41 mm. To those not familiar with the watch world, this may seem inconsequential, but to watch buyers this equates to being sent, at best, a suit that doesn’t fit, and at worst an entirely different outfit.

This grave error wasn’t remedied with the offer of a refund or a swap for the correct size, but instead the proposal of a small discount on a future purchase. It’s still very much “buyer beware” in the world of super clones.

Still, the entire process, from crypto payment to QC evaluation on Reddit to the shipper-tracked watches arriving, had taken less than a month. For the princely sum of $1,704, we had not one, but three utterly convincing replica Rolexes, even if one was completely the wrong size.

For a thorough expert evaluation of our cloned watches, WIRED met Adrian Hailwood at the UK offices of Watch Collecting, an online watch auction platform he helped launch in 2021, and for which he now provides authentication services. Since much of the production cost of super clones goes on the dial, Hailwood suggested inspecting other parts of the watch.

Under the jeweler’s loupe, he spotted bracelet screws that “really aren’t very round,” and the underside of a clasp that “is very much raw metal” and “not particularly nice.” These imperfections were followed by a Rolex logo on the bracelet which had been “milled out quite amateurishly … Almost looks like someone has done it with a Dremel.”

Hailwood plowed on. “The luminous material looks like it’s not set particularly nicely … The pip is not centered in the triangle, and it’s slightly too yellow for a modern watch.”

One startling piece of accuracy, however, is the coronet (Rolex’s crown-like logo), which since the early 2000s has been laser-etched discreetly into the 6 o’clock position of the sapphire crystal. A couple of millimeters wide and only visible under bright light, the supposed anti-counterfeit measure was present in our replica Submariner. On some fakes the coronet is fudged with a sticker or crudely scratched into the back of the sapphire. Other times it seems genuine, but fails to match the original, which is made up of tiny stars of varying sizes, not just the etched dots of the counterfeit.

Opening the watch revealed a replica movement that looked, at first glance, very much like the real deal. It appeared to be “reasonably good,” but then Hailwood pointed out how there’s a balance regulating arm to help fine-tune how quickly the watch runs—a type of movement that Rolex hasn’t used since 1957. Rolex now uses movements with free-sprung balances, so, in a bid to fool authenticators, counterfeiters have been known to swap the whole assembly around, obscuring the balance components. “That caught a lot of people out,” Hailwood says.

Since WIRED’s watches were examined, however, the counterfeiters have already upped their game. Hailwood claims free-sprung balances have now been introduced across clone movements imitating those by Rolex, Patek Philippe, Richard Mille, and Audemars Piguet. Once a relatively small-volume upgrade, these are now “industrialized features” that eliminate one of the tells he identified in our replica Submariner.

“The investment to produce this kind of clone movement … this is not back-alley sweatshop stuff,” says Hailwood, “this is big factories investing millions to produce full-on clones. It’s said by some watchmakers that these are now close enough that they can be serviced with Rolex parts, which does raise the specter of someone taking a genuine Rolex balance out and swapping it in [to a fake].”

Can there ever be justification for owning a replica watch? The community claims so. Most commonly it’s a love of the design backed up by a simple “because I can.” Some profess to own the real thing and simply want to see how closely they can match it with a fake.

Others suggest they’re a good option for people in watch-crime hot spots such as London or Milan, where it’s too dangerous to wear the real deal out in the open. The preferred approach is to lock the genuine article in a safe at home and strap a replica to your wrist when out in public. In this manner, the super clone morphs into some form of luxury decoy or insurance policy.

This works in the art world, where billionaires are urged not to display real Monets on yachts, and among the very highest echelons of classic car collecting, where insurers would rather you don’t take your $50 million Ferrari on the racetrack. In both cases, an exact replica can be a sensible solution.

Of course, it’s not just moped-riding watch thieves—there’s an illicit secondary market to be fed. Counterfeit watches are used in bait-and-switch scams where photos of a real watch are shown to a buyer who then ends up with the fake. The same trick is played on pawnbrokers, who are fed a string of legitimate watches before being duped by a knockoff.

According to a May 2025 report from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, the global fake goods trade was worth $467 billion in 2021—the most recent data available—and accounts for 2.3 percent of all global trade, rising to 4.7 percent in the European Union. Clothing, footwear, and leather goods are the most commonly seized counterfeit goods, while watches rank fifth by quantity, and first, comfortably, by value.

A second OECD report focused on Switzerland found that, also in 2021, around $4.7 billion worth of counterfeit goods infringed Swiss trademarks, leading to a $3 billion loss in domestic sales. More than 40 percent of those goods, by value, are watches, with roughly 65 percent of seizures originating in China and Hong Kong. Overall, the global fake Swiss watch market equates to about 7.7 percent of the value of Switzerland's legitimate watch exports, but with far lower production costs and sales prices per unit.

But remember, these figures are based on seized goods, not those that slip through the postal system unnoticed.

Imposter Syndrome

This should be black-and-white. Producing and selling counterfeit goods is a crime. The legality of buying, importing, and wearing them, however, varies by jurisdiction. Engaging in this industry can fairly be described as intellectual property theft, deceptive, and unethical.

One might question why buyers and wearers of counterfeit watches are pretending to be someone, or something, they aren’t. The options available for the budget watch collector have never been better. If they simply love watches, why not spend the same money on an interesting Seiko? Or, if a new genuine Rolex is beyond one’s budget, one of the brand’s certified pre-owned pieces offers an alternative to a collection of fakes.

The Reddit moderator we spoke to, who collects genuine luxury watches as well as replicas, says their love for these faux timepieces comes from being a watch fan. “I like the variety of watches that replicas allow me to have, and I like the ‘try before you buy’ that replicas afford me in some cases.”

Reddit’s own guidelines state that the selling or promoting of counterfeit goods may be considered a violation of the site’s trademark policy. The moderators of some other watch-centric subreddits have banned the discussion of counterfeit watches and parts, but for the communities reported here there seems to be little acknowledgment of wrongdoing.

In response to a request for comment, Reddit issued a statement to WIRED that says “counterfeit merchandise is covered by our Trademark Policy, which includes instructions for rightsholders who wish to file a report. We review and respond to all valid reports from rightsholders and take appropriate action on content that violates our policy.” Reddit’s Trademark Policy states that it “may ban users who repeatedly violate” it. “We may also ban subreddits after multiple removals of violative content or where it is clear that the subreddit is dedicated to violative content.”

Ultimately, what’s most striking isn’t merely the scale of this barely hiding counterfeit industry, but the misplaced enthusiasm driving it. These are real watch lovers who have built a genuine online community—people who are fluent in reference numbers, obsessing over index alignment and lume color. They are thrilled to share their knowledge and time, for free, with curious newcomers. It’s very much a genuine passion for watchmaking, but like the crooked hands of a red-lighted replica, it’s pointing the wrong way.

Our dive into the world of super clones showed us that something far more fundamental is at play here. We found that handling and wearing these timepieces brought near zero enjoyment. We love watches, from low-end to high. Buying your first Rolex or Omega, having saved for years, is a landmark achievement. It serves as a reminder of what the owner has managed to accomplish along the way—the destination of a hard-fought journey. A counterfeit, even one that looks so good it fools Rolex store staff and is classified as NWBIG by a stranger on Reddit, ultimately fails to offer joy that’s more than skin deep.

entries.title: Dell XPS 13 vs. MacBook Neo: A Surprising Upset
entries.summary: The Dell XPS 13 and MacBook Neo are both premium-feeling laptops with only 8 GB of RAM. Which $700 laptop is the better buy?
entries.content:
Ever since the MacBook Neo was announced this spring, I've been looking for a serious alternative. Not a cheap knockoff that sacrifices quality for price. No, no. I was hunting for a Windows laptop with the same goal as the MacBook Neo—hiding its compromises and delivering an otherwise premium laptop at a lower cost. For months, it was crickets.

Then, the Dell XPS 13 showed up on my doorstep, and it understood the assignment. For many reasons, this was the one I'd been waiting for. But the question remains: Is it actually the better budget laptop? The answer surprised me when I dug into the testing.

Hidden Compromises

When the MacBook Neo was originally announced, it was a shocker. Apple coming in at the $599 price point for the base configuration felt unreal. Apple had never in its history brought the MacBook to such a low price. Even at its new $699 starting price, it's in unprecedented territory. Importantly, this encroached on the territory of Windows laptops, where it has traditionally had a monopoly.

And while many Windows laptops are available at this price, they suffer from many of the same problems, such as cheap materials or corners cut with low-quality displays and touchpads. Even a cheap laptop I like quite a bit, like the HP OmniBook 5 (with the Snapdragon X Plus), has a weak point in its touchpad.

But the Dell XPS 13 sought to match the MacBook Neo's premium quality in nearly every aspect. It has the same starting price of $699 (or $599 for students). It's exactly the same size at just a half-inch thick, so when the lid is closed and you're holding it, it feels just as portable. The XPS 13 weighs 2.2 pounds, half a pound lighter than the MacBook Neo. The Neo isn't heavy, but holding both in your hands, the difference is noticeable. That's the first point in favor of the XPS 13.

Despite a slightly smaller screen (13 inches, measured diagonally), the MacBook Neo sits taller than the XPS 13 when the lid is open. That's because the XPS 13's 13.4-inch display is surrounded by much smaller bezels—particularly the bottom, which gives the XPS 13 a more modern look. The white keyboard and flashier color options of the MacBook Neo certainly have their appeal, especially since the XPS 13 comes in only two shades of silver. But in general, more screen real estate and smaller dimensions are preferable, especially if you want to travel on an airplane with your laptop.

And then there's the screen itself. Most $700 laptops have mediocre screens that aren't bright enough and have poor colors. I never expected Apple to skimp on the display, of course, and it didn't. It goes up to 509 nits (as tested) and has decent color reproduction. But the XPS 13 is better in three ways. First, it has a touchscreen, which MacBooks don't (yet) have. That's a nice addition for an entry-level model. It also has a 120-Hz refresh rate, which gives the screen fast, fluid responsiveness that not even the MacBook Air has. Again, that's a feature that's exceedingly rare to find on a budget-level laptop. Lastly, the XPS 13 has better color saturation, specifically on the Adobe RGB and P3 color scales. It's actually one of the better IPS screens I've tested on a laptop, and it's as sharp as the MacBook Neo.

None of these are weak points of the MacBook Neo, but it's worth noting that the XPS 13 has it beat in a number of these areas. That's also true of the keyboard and trackpad. Both are excellent on these laptops, and I found myself comfortable using them right off the bat. Again, trackpads in particular can be a sore spot for budget Windows laptops, but Dell smartly didn't skimp on it. Apple's the one that compromised on the keyboard, both by not including Touch ID in the base model and by removing backlighting (which the XPS 13 includes).

Ports, Storage, and Videoconferencing

I already mentioned the display and the portability, but there are a few other places where the XPS 13 is the clear winner. The first is the USB-C ports. Both devices have two, but the XPS 13 splits them, so one is on the left side, and one is on the right side. I really like this decision, as it allows you to charge the device from either side. Then, there's the speed of these USB-C ports. One of the USB-C ports on the MacBook Neo is an outdated USB 2 port. Not only is it slow for file transfers, but it also can't natively output to an external display. Both USB-C ports on the XPS 13 are USB 3.2 Gen 2, which can each support a 4K display and transfer data at up to 10 Gbps.

The Neo does have an advantage when it comes to ports, though. It has a headphone jack, whereas the XPS 13 doesn't. This might be less of a big deal today than it was in the past, but I prefer laptops to keep them.

The XPS 13 comes with 512 GB of storage in both the base and upgraded models. The MacBook Neo base model comes only with 256 GB, and you'll need to upgrade to the Touch ID model for 521 GB. On top of that, Dell's laptop uses faster storage. That's a winning combination.

The videoconferencing setup is similarly good. Both webcams are 1080p. Though the image processing is a bit better on the MacBook Neo, the XPS 13 includes an IR camera for logging in without a password. The base configuration of the Neo doesn't have Touch ID, so you have to type a password to log in, change settings, and pay online.

The RAM Problem

Apple never claimed the MacBook Neo was a powerhouse. Built on an iPhone chip (the A18 Pro) and limited to 8 GB of RAM, it is clearly designed for college students and anyone with lower-level computing needs. When I tested it initially, I found that if I wasn't paying attention, it was easy to let open applications, tons of browser tabs, and background tasks slow the computer down, with the main bottleneck being the 8 GB of RAM. Apple hasn't sold a MacBook with 8 GB of RAM since 2024, but the company has always insisted that its unified memory system means it doesn't need as much capacity as a Windows PC. But is that really true? Now that we have a very comparable Windows system with 8 GB of RAM as well, it'll be easy to test just how true Apple's claims are.

The bad news is that both devices took very little effort to use up the available memory. Playing a YouTube video with various news sites open in six Google Chrome tabs was enough to use over 90 percent of the 8 GB. Neither Windows nor macOS feels optimized for a computer with just 8 GB of RAM these days, no doubt from all the AI-infused tasks running in the background. Now, just because you're getting dangerously close to reaching 100 percent of the memory utilization, that doesn't mean your computer instantly freezes up. It takes a lot to get these systems to grind to a halt, but with a 16-GB laptop, you'll spend much less time managing what tabs and applications you have open. On the other hand, if you're a student coming from a cheap Chromebook or hand-me-down computer, these laptops will feel like a nice upgrade.

The XPS 13 has a fan inside, while the MacBook Neo is passively cooled. Under a heavy load you can hear that fan spin up in the XPS 13, whereas the Neo is completely silent. Both laptops get excellent battery life—enough to get through a full day of class or work. That's another area where laptops at this price tended to suffer in the past.

But the big difference between these two laptops is how you can configure them. Both start at $700 ($699 for the Neo, to be exact), and you get one upgrade option. For an extra $100, you can move up to the MacBook Neo with 512 GB of storage and Touch ID built in. On the other hand, the Dell XPS 13 has a $900 model that's identical to the base model, except it has 16 GB of RAM. So yes, the 16-GB version of the XPS 13 is $100 more expensive. But it's better in nearly every way, and it's likely the best laptop you can buy for less than $1,000.

And even when comparing the 8-GB model, the XPS 13 handily beats the MacBook Neo in tons of small ways. It has a better display, a backlit keyboard, two USB ports—one on each side—that support charging and 4K monitors, and it's more portable. It does all that while looking super sharp and feeling just as premium as the Neo. While I think everyone should buy a 16-GB laptop, at the 8-GB level, the Dell XPS 13 is the better laptop no matter how you slice it.

entries.title: There’s a Very Simple Reason Why You Love the Slate Truck
entries.summary: The car world is filled with designers still obsessed with shoehorning sex into their rides. Slate went a different route, and it’s why people are smitten with the charming electric pickup.
entries.content:
Tisha Johnson is a rare anomaly in the car world: a design leader for an automaker who is not a man. In a resolutely testosterone-fueled industry where, traditionally, women have seemingly been given positions of authority in design labs as long as they focus on interiors, colors, or material selections, very few have been afforded free rein on the most important visual element of the car, the exterior, let alone promoted to run the entire aesthetic show. Johnson has.

As head of design at Slate, this gender-specific fact might be why the world has fallen in love with the Jeff Bezos–backed truck. Casual observers might put the Slate EV's popularity down to its low price. Starting at $24,950, the Slate arriving later this year won't just be the cheapest EV on the US market; it will also be the cheapest pickup truck of any power flavor.

But people buy cheap all the time. Be it a pickup or portable speaker, cheap doesn't mean they love the product; it usually means a compromise. And it's hard to love a compromise. The real trick is in creating something beautiful and accessible.

It's a hard task—ask Jony Ive, who has fashioned the best-looking automotive interior in decades for the $640,000 Ferrari Luce. Even though you could buy 25 (and a half) Slate trucks for the same price as a Luce, the Ferrari's exterior has been met with a frosty reception, to say the least. The budget Slate, meanwhile, has won multiple awards for its looks, not just for how much it costs. Johnson and her team have nailed beautiful and accessible. The TL;DR secret sauce? Ditch the testosterone and bring in a woman's perspective, and, perhaps more importantly, lack of ego.

Johnson has been working toward getting people to love the Slate for 27 years. Her final-year thesis at California’s Art Center College of Design in 1999 focused on the genuine need for a useful, affordable, and hopefully desirable vehicle for a single mom. It has taken two long spells at Volvo (a 17-year tour in total), with stints in between as head of design at Whirlpool and Herman Miller, to realize her vision.

Toward the end of this year, Slate's first customers will get behind the wheel of Johnson's dream of an astonishingly affordable vehicle—one that can transform from an electric truck to a traditional “squareback” SUV to a jeep-like “fastback” SUV, thanks to a genuinely ingenious modular design. Complete color changes will be possible in two days and cost just $500. Panels can be swapped out; decals, roof racks, and $60 grille plates can be bought from Slate or, as the company is going to publish a load of its 3D files, tweaked and printed by owners themselves. Many companies talk about genuinely democratic design; very few deliver.

I sat down with Johnson to discuss this rare and laudable woman-centric approach to the Slate, and exactly how it's brought about an EV that the design world, auto trade, and the general public (180,000 preorders and counting) all love.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

JEREMY WHITE: Pickups are trapped in a hyper-masculine, aggressive design language. Giant grilles, towering fronts, hostile postures. As a woman leading the truck's design team, was stepping away from that intentional pushback against car-guy tropes or a byproduct of creating a utility vehicle with empathy and affordability?

TISHA JOHNSON: We were always intentional in what the expression would be. There were definitely things that we didn't want it to be. We didn't want it to be a jerk. We literally said that. First and foremost, we wanted the vehicle to be truly approachable. Friendly but very confident. We all attach to the vehicles we drive. They represent our personality, our self-expression. This vehicle, the ability to personalize, is a cornerstone of the thinking here.

We talked about—before we actually ever had one line sketched—that you're walking through the parking lot; you've been shopping, and you look and see your vehicle. How do you feel? How do you feel when you see a Slate? You feel like you cannot wait to get back to that vehicle, and it's a vehicle you can count on. It's someone you can trust. These were the kinds of things we wanted to see. We didn't want it to be cliché or look at the past. We said it would be familiar, but at the same time feel very relevant today.

Having written your thesis on designing a vehicle for a single mom with kids, starting from a different goal than a male designer, what tangible design decisions does your team bring to the Slate to create a truck for everyone, not just men? Did a different design language have to be established?

I want to make sure I'm super clear with you: We absolutely rejected an overly aggressive, hyper-dominant look. We didn't want it to look like a beast on the road. No way. Look at the front fascia, where the headlamps are. The face of the vehicle—it has eyes wide open. Round headlamps. There are reasons why this is good for accessorizing; it's very easy to get to and put different headlamps there if you want—but it also has an alertness to it that we wanted. But if you look at where that hood line is, it strikes across part of that headlamp, and that is so that there is definitely an expression of overt confidence.

Look at the side mirror; there's an area there where we put a little landing pad for a small decal. If you had only a few bucks in your pocket, and you just wanted to give a little pop of expression or color right there, you could. I just love that.

I would argue that a woman is not looking for a vehicle designed for her. Research shows our buying behaviors are not focused on anything clichéd, that's for sure. So we made that face come off as confident, fair, and modern, and with more product-like attributes than other vehicles.

Then you go from there. On the surface, there's a really nice strong shoulder. That is a cue that there's a vehicle there that's safe and reliable. We didn't get into a lot of surfacing that is swoopy and arrowed. The angle of the windscreen is fairly upright. We didn't go all super-fast there. These are decisions rejecting the tropes expected in a vehicle today. These modern clichés, we just left those behind.

Considering you rejected the design clichés, are you surprised at the plaudits that Slate’s looks have garnered from the male-dominated auto design world?

I'll give you a little bit of behind-the-scenes. We started with some assumptions that you would find any design group considering, like putting precious materials in the front area; and this is where we'll put the name mark, the DNA, and it is placed there beautifully, never to be touched, just to be admired. That's what goes on in a design studio.

As we were looking at designs and testing internally, we could see what people were attracted to. But as a design group, we kept saying, “This isn't right yet.” Then finally we realized the problem: We were using the exact playbook that has been handed down from generation to generation. We literally said, “This is all wrong. We cannot do this.”

So we literally threw out that playbook and said, if this is Slate's DNA, then we're going to put a plate right there between those two headlamps that has exposed fasteners. Yes, it holds the main brand mark, but we designed it in such a way that it's easy to remove, easy to replace. Yes, we offer some different designs, but we're saying this is easy enough for you, as the owner, to 3D-print something to put here if you want to. Now, that's outrageous. That is different.

Absolutely we wanted to forge a new path. We just did not know that it would be recognized. We didn't think it would be. We weren't considering it being appreciated so quickly and by so many. That's been an honor for us as a team.

EV development has been hijacked by tech-bro posturing. Ludicrous acceleration; giant screens. Is stripping away unnecessary tech bloat fundamentally an exercise in empathetic, less ego-driven design? And how do you take the ego out of auto design when it seems to be impossible at almost every other car brand?

Yes, I wish I could say it better. Before we had the design, we had some principles that were core, and one of those was to take away all of the unnecessary tech. It drives up the cost, yes, but I was driving in a car with my niece and her friends, a mix of twentysomething men and women, but mostly women. They were taking jabs at the tech-bro culture and talking about how it was getting in the way of the simple pleasures and things that you could appreciate. They said, “Like all of these screens everywhere. I don't use them. I'm not interested in it at all.” I was in heaven hearing it.

We considered radical things like, do you really need an HVAC unit? It wasn't a provocative idea that somebody put on the table to make a point. It was fiercely debated, and it won for good reasons. But the integrated stereo system did not win. We did a cost analysis on the window crank against a power pack, and the window crank won.

I infused a word into the design process. It wasn't overtly in the first description of the Slate, but it was there, between the lines. The word was “love.” That's a word we felt in the design studio, because we understood that as we were starting—the descriptions of the vehicle being affordable, easy to own, personalized, something that was robust and something that you wanted that was cool. You put that all together? That spells love.

So we wanted to be very open that we wanted people to love the vehicle. It requires real commitment on all of those levels at the same time. These are natural tensions that, in any other program I've ever worked on, at some point you let go of one of those big ideas to get to the goal on time. We said no.

In so much other car design, the word is not love; it's sex. Phallic fronts, power bulges. Car designers generally don't talk of lovable cars, do they?

Just being candid, I've been in design reviews in my earlier years where I would feel the conversation completely left my point of view out—the point of view of actually most people. We know that a female in the household is driving decisionmaking around a car purchase. She doesn't want to be classified or catered to in a way that is cliché. She does want to be considered, and that's important, because a woman will be inclined to consider the needs of everyone in the household. Letting all of that “gender” into vehicle design? I've always thought it was kind of silly. Love is so much more stable, Jeremy.

And lasts longer.

It does. You would see female designers more likely to be color and material designers on the interior. More and more, you are seeing a more equal distribution of men and women around different topics in car development, and that's great. But the conversation used to go, “Well, once you get inside of the vehicle, then you have the emotional bond, and it's more of an animal attraction on the outside.” I really push back on that. Yes, there is an attraction [with the Slate]. But that attraction that draws you toward it is based on something that is very lasting from the inside out. It's a deeper emotional connection.

How do you think you'll feel when you see your first mom driving around with two kids in the back of her Slate?

Emotional. It's very emotional to think about that. It's something I wanted to do, and I just hated that I didn't do it. And so, every day, I'm motivated because I'm involved in the act of doing that, of realizing that. It's incredibly rewarding.

entries.title: Reverse-Lookup Service Exposed Millions of Photos of People’s Faces
entries.summary: The people-search tool ClarityCheck says its reverse image search service is “private and secure”—but it left a database containing more than 9 million image files exposed.
entries.content:
When someone uploads a photo to the people-search tool ClarityCheck, the website has a clear message: “Your reverse image search is private and secure.” New research, though, shows that the website left more than 9 million image files, including photographs of people’s faces, publicly exposed. And a second misconfiguration publicly exposed people’s email addresses and phone numbers.

Overall, according to findings from independent security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, the exposed ClarityCheck database contained roughly 450 GB of images, including what appeared to be profile images, screenshots, and other photographs of adults, teenagers, and children. All of the images were stored in an unsecured Amazon S3 bucket, with files in folders named “faces” and “profiles,” which could be accessed by anyone online through a URL included in the company’s publicly available website code.

ClarityCheck is one of a number of so-called people-finder tools that have appeared online in recent years. These websites broadly claim to be able to search the web, public records, and other databases to identify individuals. ClarityCheck’s website says it can run searches on phone numbers, email addresses, vehicle identification numbers, and names. Its photo-search page says it can help “identify anyone in a photo” and find social media profiles “in seconds.”

While ClarityCheck secured the giant image database after WIRED contacted the company in July, Fowler warns that it was seemingly exposed for months, and his initial efforts to flag the problem to the company were unsuccessful. Accidental data exposures create risk for any personal information, but particularly for sensitive and unchangeable biometric data like face images.

And while ClarityCheck’s website requires people to attest that they have permission to upload photos to its site, Fowler points out that in practice, people whose faces were exposed may have had no idea that ClarityCheck held their image. After all, he notes, the service is explicitly designed for identification, and people don’t typically seek to identify themselves or people they know.

“If you’re trying to find out who a person is, you might not have authorization or permission, so people might not know that their image had been dumped into this database that was public,” Fowler tells WIRED. “An AI bot could crawl it, extract faces, and use them for training. And there are lots of pictures of kids in there.”

In a statement sent to WIRED, a spokesperson said that ClarityCheck appreciated Fowler’s efforts to alert the company about the issues. “Once this was drawn to the attention of the appropriate teams, we acted immediately to restrict access,” the spokesperson said.

The company disputed any characterization that the data was “exposed,” saying that an “ordinary member of the public” would not have come across it. “We do not accept that data in the temporary storage location was ‘publicly exposed,’ which implies large-scale public access,” the spokesperson says. “Access required knowledge of a specific, unindexed URL that was not discoverable through ordinary use of the ClarityCheck service or a general web search.”

The security industry broadly, as well as the US federal government specifically, considers data to be exposed if it could be accessed by people who are not intended to have access—particularly if it is reachable on the open internet without being protected by an authentication requirement, such as a username and password. “Exposure is the state in which personal or sensitive data has been left accessible, discoverable, or otherwise put at risk of unauthorized access, whether or not anyone has yet taken or misused it,” says Mark Beare, head of consumer products at the security company Malwarebytes. “A publicly reachable database backup, a misconfigured storage bucket, or credentials sitting in a system that a researcher can reach are all exposures.”

“There is no suggestion of malicious access, as the researcher notes,” the ClarityCheck statement continued. “The data involved includes duplicate, cropped, and resized copies of the same files, along with non-image data, not 9 million unique images.”

The company added that it has “improved” its security reporting procedures to help other researchers contact the company in the future.

In addition to the face data, ClarityCheck had also misconfigured its APIs such that its website URLs could be manipulated to reveal data about people simply by entering names; anyone using any consumer browser could have done this. Entering a name into one of the URLs would return multiple potential email addresses, physical addresses, and phone numbers for people with that name. After WIRED contacted the company, the URLs were secured. The ClarityCheck spokesperson said in the statement that the details displayed were “sourced from publicly available information and licensed third-party data providers.”

ClarityCheck’s face-search feature allows people to upload an image and then receive a “report” about where that image may appear online and who may be shown in the photo. When a WIRED reporter tested the system using their own face image, the website said it was “scanning facial landmarks” and “mapping unique face geometry” before matching the image to others online and offering a report that could include a full name, addresses, location history, public appearances, photos, videos, social media profiles, and “hidden dating profiles” for a fee. The resulting report named the reporter, provided a biography, and linked to multiple photos of them online.

Misconfigurations and accidental exposures are unfortunately common online, but as digital platforms offer more and more automated capabilities for collecting and analyzing sensitive personal data, the stakes grow ever higher for securing information.

“Systems that rely on highly sensitive personal information to verify individuals will continue to carry these risks, even with stronger data minimization and security practices, because the model itself depends on collecting sensitive data,” says Rebecca Williams, director of strategy for privacy and data governance at the American Civil Liberties Union.

Fowler emphasizes that exposed data, including photos, are more valuable than ever to scammers or cybercriminals. “Let’s say I was in a criminal outfit and I was catfishing people, and I scroll through all these pictures and I pick out 20 of the most attractive people and then I just use their image and AI and I create a persona,” Fowler says.

entries.title: Hot or Not Built the Internet We’re Still Swiping Through
